title: The Basics of requirements.txt
body: requirements.txt is a file that lists the external packages required for a project. It tells you which packages need to be installed when running the same project on another computer.
detail: Small code projects that use only the Python standard library may not require a `requirements.txt` file. However, if you use packages that need to be installed separately—such as requests, pandas, or python-dotenv—you should include a list of them. This allows anyone who receives the project on a new computer or server to quickly install the necessary packages. Think of requirements.txt not as code itself, but as a file that describes the runtime environment.

title: pip install -r flow
body: "python -m pip install -r requirements.txt" is a command that installs all the packages listed in `requirements.txt` at once. It is typically run after activating a virtual environment.
detail: -r means to read the requirements file. Using the `python -m pip` syntax makes it easier to run the pip associated with the currently active Python environment. This helps reduce confusion—especially on Windows, where multiple Python installations may be present or when using venv—where pip might be installed in the wrong environment. After installing a package, you can import and use it in your code.

title: Version Locking and pip freeze
body: Exact pins reduce variation but do not by themselves fix Python, the operating system, or every transitive dependency. pip freeze can include packages installed by accident. Review direct and transitive requirements and use a suitable lock or hashes plus runtime documentation when stronger reproduction is needed.

title: Reproducible Runtime Environment
body: A virtual environment plus requirements is a basic dependency-isolation workflow. Activation is optional because the environment interpreter can be called directly. Document supported Python and OS constraints, pinning policy, and a real verification command for stronger reproducibility.
